blogs.title: The Perils of Expert Confusion: Why Self-Contradiction Cannot Save a Jury Verdict
blogs.description: This post analyzes the Federal Circuit's reversal of the infringement verdict based solely on the 'confusing and unclear' testimony of the plaintiff's expert witness. The article examines how Chief Judge Moore applied the *Johns Hopkins* precedent to hold that a party bearing the burden of proof cannot rely on an expert who offers contradictory mappings of claim limitations to hardware architecture. It explores the practical implications for litigation strategy, specifically regarding the necessity of rigorous pre-trial preparation for experts to ensure their testimony remains consistent across direct examination, cross-examination, and post-verdict arguments.

blogs.title: Claim Construction vs. Prosecution History Estoppel: The Limits of 'Three Signals'
blogs.description: Focusing on the '775 patent dispute, this blog post dissects the tension between broad claim construction and prosecution history estoppel. While the court declined to find that Finesse had surrendered coverage for devices using only two unique input signals (interpreting 'three signals' as merely 'separately identifiable'), it ultimately ruled against infringement due to a failure to prove the specific mathematical operation (seven multiplications). The analysis considers how this decision narrows the path for plaintiffs attempting to stretch numerical claim limitations beyond what is explicitly disclosed in technical documentation, emphasizing that broad construction does not excuse a lack of evidentiary mapping.

blogs.title: Substantial Evidence in Patent Trials: When Technical Documentation Fails to Match Claim Language
blogs.description: This entry investigates the Federal Circuit's strict application of the 'substantial evidence' standard when reviewing technical infringement proofs. By highlighting how Dr. Wells' reliance on Nokia documents failed because those documents described modulus and complex conjugate operations rather than the literal multiplications recited in the claims, this post discusses the critical gap often found between high-level engineering diagrams and precise patent claim language. It serves as a cautionary tale for patentees regarding the need for granular, line-by-line mapping between accused product specifications and every element of a claim, particularly in complex digital signal processing cases.
